citations.text: Haidt, J. (2012). The Righteous Mind: Why Good People Are Divided by Politics and Religion. Pantheon Books.

en.general: The theory that human moral judgment rests on a small set of evolved, shared intuitive foundations -- analogous to taste receptors -- including at least Care/Harm, Fairness/Cheating, Loyalty/Betrayal, Authority/Subversion, Purity/Degradation, and Freedom/Oppression. Everyone shares the same foundations (the 'taste receptors'), but cultures and individuals develop very different 'moral tastes' -- which foundations are emphasized, and how -- through their evolutionary heritage, cultural history, and individual socialization. Moral judgments are typically made quickly and intuitively (fast, System-1-like processing) with reasoned justification following afterward, rather than being derived from deliberate reasoning first. The same shared-foundation architecture that lets people build cooperative moral communities ('binds') also makes it easy to see other groups' differently-weighted moral intuitions as simply wrong rather than differently calibrated ('blinds'), fueling moral polarization between groups that each see themselves as good and reasonable.

examples: Two political groups disagreeing sharply on an issue because one weights the Care/Harm foundation most heavily and the other weights Authority/Subversion or Purity/Degradation more heavily -- not because one side lacks morality.
A person feeling immediate, unreasoned disgust at a norm violation (fast, intuitive judgment) and only afterward constructing a rational-sounding justification for that reaction.
